title: Memory Systems Detective
summary: Judge three claims about separable memory systems against three fictional memory profiles. For each pairing, decide whether the profile supports the claim, counts against it, or cannot decide it.
learningObjectives: State what a profile must contain before it supports a distinction between memory systems.
Distinguish the claim that two tasks are separable from the claim that two systems exist.
Explain why normal recognition with impaired recall does not establish a retrieval account.
Identify task impurity in a profile where every impaired measure shares its material.
List the non-neurological explanations of a uniformly slightly-below-average profile.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native radio and button controls throughout. The profile chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving every measure, what it asks the person to do, the distance from its own control group and its standing in words. Every bar also prints its own value, so the fill is redundant, and bars clearly outside the control range are distinguished by fill and by a wording in the table rather than by colour alone. The claim under judgement sits in a goal banner in the interactive header, so it is readable while the verdict radios at the bottom of the control column are used, and the profile chart is pinned at 294px so the evidence stays on screen. Grid cells print the verdict as a word and add the intended verdict when they differ. Every judgement announces through the shell's polite live region with a running count. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths. The grid is three claims by three profiles; a fourth profile sits inside a native <details> element in the profile fieldset, reachable by keyboard in one step and announced as collapsed rather than being disabled, and its column appears in the grid only once it has been used, so an untouched column never reads as unfinished work. Progress counts the nine core cells and reports optional judgements separately.
readmeTopic: When a memory profile supports a distinction between systems, when it counts against one, and when it cannot decide either way
simulationNotes: Three invented core profiles plus one optional fourth, with invented numbers on six invented measures, each expressed as a distance from the average of that measure's own fictional control group in control standard deviations. A measure counts as clearly below its controls at minus two or lower and as within range above about minus 1.2. The core grid, rows being the three claims and columns profiles A, B and E: short-term against episodic gives support, support, cannot; episodic against skill gives support, cannot, cannot; one general reduction gives against, against, support. Four of the nine cells support a claim, two count against one and three cannot decide. Profile A settles all three and is the only one that does, which is what makes it a textbook case rather than a typical one. The optional profile D answers cannot, cannot, against: its verbal measures are confounded with a word-knowledge loss, so an apparent dissociation cannot be pinned on the memory system it appears to implicate. The grid was five claims by five profiles until version 1.2.0. Profile C had a verdict column identical to profile A on every claim, and its one distinct contribution - the retrieval-versus-storage trap - is now the challenge task; the episodic-against-semantic row was identical to the episodic-against-skill row on every profile; and the retrieval-against-storage row was cannot in all twenty-five cells, so it never discriminated. Span with manipulation was dropped from the battery because it moved with immediate span in every profile and no claim distinguished them. Deliberate simplifications: six measures is very few, real batteries separate several things merged here, and the intended answers are judgements the tool invites the learner to argue with. No anatomy appears anywhere, because these distinctions are between what tasks require. No real person, published case, clinical instrument or syndrome name is used, and nothing on the page diagnoses anybody or offers a prognosis.
